l: GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: This document presents Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GRAG), by Yuntong Hu, Zhihan Lei, Zheng Zhang, Bo Pan, Chen Ling, and Liang Zhao. GRAG extends Retrieval-Augmented Generation for networked documents, where relevant evidence is not merely isolated text but interconnected textual graphs whose nodes and edges have text attributes. The paper argues that Large Language Models can use textual attributes but do not inherently capture complex topology, while exhaustive search for an optimal subgraph is NP-hard. GRAG frames the task as retrieving an optimal query-relevant textual subgraph from a graph and supplying it, with the query, to an LLM for generation. Its retrieval stage uses a divide-and-conquer process: it indexes K-hop ego-graphs with pre-trained language-model embeddings, ranks them by cosine similarity to the query, merges the top-N candidates, and applies Textual Subgraph Soft Pruning. Two multilayer perceptrons assign query-dependent scaling factors to nodes and edges, reducing redundant material and yielding a tailored subgraph with linear complexity. For generation, GRAG supplies complementary text and graph views. The text view turns retrieved ego-graphs into hierarchical descriptions that distinguish tree edges from additional edges. The graph view applies a Graph Neural Network to the softly pruned graph, and an MLP aligns graph embeddings with the LLM text-vector space. The resulting graph and text embeddings are concatenated with the query context for generation. Experiments on GraphQA, using WebQSP for knowledge-graph question answering and ExplaGraphs for common-sense reasoning, find that GRAG outperforms standard RAG retrievers and LLM baselines in graph multi-hop reasoning. Without LLM fine-tuning, it reaches 0.7236 Hit@1 on WebQSP and 0.9223 accuracy on ExplaGraphs; frozen LLMs with GRAG outperform fine-tuned LLMs on all reported tasks. Ablations emphasize the value of graph-aware retrieval, graph encoding, soft pruning, and hierarchical descriptions. Two-hop ego-graphs generally beat one-hop versions, but overly large subgraphs or too many retrieved entities can add irrelevant information and impair generation. The paper closes by noting that GRAG depends on effective initial node ranking and pruning, so performance can suffer when graph structure or node importance is hard to estimate.

l: GRAG, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: GRAG, Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, is a retrieval-augmented generation approach and computational framework for graph-based, graph context-aware generation. It extends traditional Retrieval-Augmented Generation by considering textual graphs in both retrieval and generation, aiming to retrieve an optimal query-relevant textual subgraph and use its textual and topological information to improve the relevance of LLM-generated content. Its central challenge is textual subgraph retrieval, where exhaustive search is NP-hard. GRAG addresses this with a divide-and-conquer, retrieval-then-pruning strategy: it retrieves important K-hop ego-graphs rather than individual entities, merges the top-N relevant ego-graphs, and applies soft pruning to reduce irrelevant graph information while preserving textual and topological information. This produces an approximately optimal subgraph, described as linear-time retrieval. In generation, GRAG supplies two complementary views of the retrieved graph: hierarchical text descriptions as hard prompts through text tokens, and graph-encoder outputs as soft prompts through graph tokens. For ExplaGraphs, whose graphs are small chains, it feeds the entire graph to the LLM and leverages topological information. Reported results show GRAG outperforming tested RAG retrievers, RAG-based LLM baselines, fine-tuned LLMs on all tasks, and LLM baselines in graph reasoning scenarios, especially multi-hop graph reasoning. It reports Hit@1 of 0.7236 on WebQSP, accuracy of 0.9223 on ExplaGraphs, and 79% valid-entity references in a small-scale human evaluation. Its retrieval may perform suboptimally when graph structure or node importance is difficult to estimate. Code and datasets are available at https://github.com/HuieL/GRAG.

l: Naive Retrieval-Augmented Generation, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Naive Retrieval-Augmented Generation retrieves individual documents using retrievers such as BM25, MiniLM-L12-v2, and G-Retriever. It improves LLM performance over an LLM-only baseline, but lacks topological information and underperforms graph-aware approaches for networked documents.

l: networked documents, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Networked documents are textual data linked by relationships, appearing in citation graphs, social media, and knowledge graphs. Unlike isolated documents, their connections matter for comprehensive retrieval and context-aware answers. The account begins with their real-world applications, then explains why Naive Retrieval-Augmented Generation, focused on individual documents, is difficult.

l: textual subgraphs, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: A textual subgraph is a subgraph structure in a textual graph, defined by subsets of nodes and edges and their natural-language attributes. It is the retrieval target of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation rather than discrete entities or individual documents. Its high-dimensional textual nodes and edges make selecting the subgraph that maximizes generation quality a combinatorial optimization problem. Beginning with selected important or key nodes, it unfolds as a union of induced partial neighborhoods and selected K-hop neighbors. For a relevant query, GRAG retrieves an approximate optimal textual subgraph through divide-and-conquer, K-hop ego-graphs, and soft pruning in linear time.

l: large language model, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Large Language Models (LLMs) are language models that perform graph-based reasoning and can encode textual node and edge attributes, supporting classification, knowledge graph creation, graph reasoning, and zero-shot graph answering. They demonstrate graph reasoning especially with hierarchical text structures, but training on large text corpora does not inherently provide understanding of complex graph-structured data because text lacks explicit topological information. They also struggle with factual errors owing to training-data limitations and lack of real-time knowledge. GRAG addresses these limits by providing textual graphs through complementary text and graph views, including concatenated graph and text embeddings, to improve understanding of relationships and guide generation. Through these views, LLMs more effectively comprehend and utilize graph context; a frozen LLM enhanced by GRAG can outperform fine-tuned LLMs with reduced training cost.

l: graph context, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Graph context is incorporated into generation through textual and topological information represented in text and graph views. GRAG uses this context to enhance generation and support multi-hop reasoning on textual graphs. Graph context is incorporated into both the retrieval and generation stages of GRAG. It is represented through hierarchical text descriptions and graph-based soft prompts so that LLMs can use relationships and topology alongside textual information.

l: text view, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: The text view converts textual graphs, including retrieved textual ego-graphs, into hierarchical descriptions used as hard prompts with queries, preserving narrated connections and textual and topological information for the large language model.

s: Graph-based reasoning is identified as a task on which Large Language Models have demonstrated capabilities. The unit evaluates GRAG in graph reasoning scenarios and reports that it outperforms RAG-based retrievers and LLM baselines. LLM contextual reasoning capabilities benefit graph reasoning. Some graph retrieval problems can be simplified into reasoning chains that retrieve the path between a question and a target entity.

l: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Retrieval-Augmented Generation is a generation method that retrieves external data for LLMs, reducing factual errors, unlike traditional text-similarity document retrieval, which does not explicitly account for document networks.

l: textual graph, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: A textual graph is a graph of networked documents with text-attributed nodes and edges, formally represented by node and edge sets and their natural-language attributes. It preserves textual and topological information for GRAG retrieval and generation. Graph G supplies subgraphs: its K-hop ego-graphs are indexed and ranked as candidate textual subgraphs, then semantically relevant candidates are retrieved and refined for a query. Retrieved subgraphs become hierarchical descriptions and graph embeddings. For LLMs, the graph is presented through complementary graph and text views to provide graph context.

l: divide-and-conquer strategy, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: The divide-and-conquer strategy retrieves the most relevant K-hop ego-graphs around top-ranked important nodes, treating their union as the subgraph. It approximates textual relevance by summing neighborhood scores, then uses soft pruning to refine and union these partial neighborhoods toward the optimal textual subgraph.

l: ego-graphs, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: An ego-graph is a K-hop neighborhood centered on a node, uniquely identified, encoded, indexed, and retrieved by GRAG for queries. It differs from a tree through additional within-level or cross-level edges: Breadth-First Search extracts its rooted tree part, Tg, while Eg holds non-tree edges. GRAG searches these graphs; 2-hop versions outperform 1-hop ones in the reported WebQSP study, whereas larger subgraphs may cost more time, oversmooth, and add irrelevant information.

l: Textual Subgraph Soft Pruning, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Textual Subgraph Soft Pruning is a mechanism that minimizes irrelevant nodes and edges in retrieved textual subgraphs before they are encoded into graph tokens. Using Multilayer Perceptrons, it ranks entities by distance from the query and softly masks farther ones with scalars nearer 0. It is especially important for dense graphs, though difficult importance estimates can impair retrieval.

l: hard prompts, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: It concatenates the query and hierarchical description of the textual subgraph, then is provided to the large language model.

l: soft prompts, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Soft prompts are task-adapted prompt embeddings formed from soft pruned subgraph representations, preserving graph connections, controlling message passing, and informing generation.

l: Graph Neural Network, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Graph Neural Network encodes graph topological information and graph context through graph tokens, performing message passing over node and edge features with learned relevance scaling. As a graph encoder, it embeds retrieved context for the LLM; removing it lowers WebQSP Hit@1, showing textual relationship descriptions are insufficient.

l: fine-tuned LLM, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: has_accuracy 33.94% [on ExplaGraphs without retrieval] The LLM performs poorly when all graph information is placed in the prompt without retrieval, showing that redundant graph information can harm generation. GRAG substantially improves its performance without requiring fine-tuning, while fine-tuning provides only marginal additional gains when GRAG is already used.

s: A hierarchical description is a text representation of an ego-graph. It uses indentation and nested nodes to express graph levels, retain node text or titles, and make parent-child relationships and connectivity explicit. It is produced by pre-order traversal, appending node and edge texts with a relation template, then inserting remaining edge texts, enabling lossless conversion while preserving topology.

s: Textual subgraph retrieval seeks to maximize generation quality by selecting important nodes, retrieving offline-encoded K-hop neighborhoods, ranking candidate ego-graphs by semantic relevance to a query, and refining selected neighborhoods. It reduces redundant graph information and favors topology-aware textual subgraphs over text-only retrieval, but too many subgraphs can hurt performance. Its efficiency and quality depend on initial node ranking and pruning, especially when structure or importance is hard to estimate.

s: A neighborhood consists of a node and selected nodes within K hops. GRAG encodes neighborhoods surrounding each node offline, retrieves promising candidates, and prunes them into query-relevant subgraphs.

l: Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: The document presents K-RagRec, a knowledge-graph retrieval-augmented framework for Large Language Model–based recommender systems. Shijie Wang and colleagues focus on two central weaknesses of LLM recommendations: hallucinations and lack of current, domain-specific knowledge. While Retrieval-Augmented Generation can supplement language models with external information, the paper argues that vanilla RAG may retrieve noisy or incomplete text and fail to capture structural relationships important for recommendation. K-RagRec instead retrieves reliable, up-to-date knowledge sub-graphs from item knowledge graphs. It constructs hop-field sub-graphs, semantically indexes them, selectively decides whether to retrieve information according to item popularity, and reranks retrieved sub-graphs. Graph neural networks encode the selected structures, and an MLP projector maps them into the frozen LLM’s embedding space as soft prompts. Only the GNNs and projector are trained with cross-entropy loss; the LLM remains frozen. This graph-based design is intended to supply structural information without requiring long context inputs. The paper situates the approach among RAG methods such as REALM, RETRO, and DPR, noting that graph-based retrieval has been used to provide structured, faithful knowledge and reduce hallucinations, but remains under-explored for recommendation. Experiments on MovieLens-1M, MovieLens-20M, and Amazon Book evaluate K-RagRec with LLama-2-7b, LLama-3-8b, and QWEN2-7b against inference-only, prompt-tuning, and LoRA fine-tuning baselines. Under leave-one-out candidate ranking, K-RagRec delivers the strongest or near-strongest results in most settings on Accuracy and Recall@3/5, and popularity-selective retrieval reduces inference time. Ablations show the importance of graph encoding, retrieval, thresholds, and sub-graph counts. The study is limited to 7b and 8b models, Freebase as the sole external knowledge graph, and popularity-based selection. Future work proposes larger models, additional knowledge graphs, and flexible retrieval policies such as reinforcement learning. The work received support from the Hong Kong Research Grants Council and The Hong Kong Polytechnic University.

l: recommender systems, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: Recommender systems are techniques and systems that help people make daily decisions and alleviate information overload across user-oriented online services. They matter in online shopping, job matching, and social media, where they have gained impact. Their development progresses rapidly alongside Large Language Models, including K-RagRec for improving recommendation generation.

l: Large Language Models, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: Large Language Models are large models that acquire broad knowledge and exceptional language-understanding capabilities through training on extensive, wide-ranging data. They can support next-generation recommender systems by interpreting user profiles, item descriptions, and historical interactions. Their use is limited by hallucinations and insufficient up-to-date or domain-specific knowledge. In K-RagRec, a frozen model receives recommendation prompts and historical items, optionally with retrieved knowledge sub-graphs, and generates recommendations. Retrieved knowledge graphs help it use structural information without long context input.

l: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: Retrieval-Augmented Generation is a method and generative-AI technology that leverages external knowledge sources or databases to supply an LLM with specific, relevant, and up-to-date knowledge. It retrieves fragments from a large corpus or external knowledge base to guide generation, combining retrieval systems with language models to produce coherent and informative text. This can enhance LLM understanding and generation, mitigate hallucinations and knowledge gaps, and enable effective recommendations without costly fine-tuning. However, vanilla or standard methods can introduce unnecessary noise, overlook structural relationships in knowledge, and fail to retrieve all relevant textual chunks because of harmful document disturbance.

l: knowledge graph, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: A knowledge graph is a graph-based external knowledge database and structured, factual, editable representation of knowledge. It contains entities, relations, and factual triples, providing high-quality, up-to-date structure information. It serves as a faithful source for recommendations and generation: item-related knowledge or knowledge sub-graphs can be retrieved to improve recommendation performance and augment large language models. In K-RagRec, graph neural network and pretrained language model indexing supports coarse- and fine-grained retrieval.

l: K-RagRec, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: K-RagRec is a knowledge retrieval-augmented framework for large language model recommendation. It augments recommendation generation with reliable, up-to-date knowledge and structure information from external item knowledge graphs, while avoiding long context input through expressive graph encoding. Its five components are hop-field knowledge sub-graph semantic indexing, popularity selective retrieval, knowledge sub-graph retrieval, knowledge sub-graph re-ranking, and knowledge-augmented recommendation. It first constructs a vector database by coarse- and fine-granularity indexing of knowledge sub-graphs, using a graph neural network and a pretrained language model; SentenceBert encodes entities, relations, and query attributes. A popularity selective policy determines items to retrieve, then it retrieves the top three most similar sub-graphs for each item and reranks five sub-graphs to prioritize relevant results. A GNN Encoder encodes retrieved sub-graph structure, and a projector aligns the sub-graphs with the LLM semantic space, providing them as soft prompts to a frozen large language model. Implemented with PyTorch and run on two NVIDIA A6000-48GB GPUs, it is effective on three real-world datasets. It outperforms GraphToken w/ RAG and G-retriever with prompt tuning across evaluated datasets and backbones, achieves its best performance with LoRA fine-tuning, and is efficient compared with KG-Text on MovieLens-1M with LLama-2-7b, where it records 1.06 seconds per inference.

l: hallucinations, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: is_a significant challenge for LLM-based recommender systems Hallucinations can cause LLM-based recommender systems to generate entirely fictional recommendations, such as suggesting the non-existent film "Godmother" after a user watched "The Godfather". Retrieval from external knowledge sources is presented as a way to mitigate this problem.

l: structure information, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: is_a information [high-quality and up-to-date; retrieved from the knowledge graph] Structure information from an external knowledge graph is retrieved to augment recommendations. K-RagRec incorporates this information into the recommendation generation process.

l: LLM-based recommender systems, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: LLM-based recommender systems are a new recommendation paradigm that uses Large Language Models’ language understanding and generalization to capture nuanced user preferences and generate recommendations. Their central challenge is that they can hallucinate or produce fictional recommendations and lack up-to-date, domain-specific knowledge, partly because recommendation-oriented training corpora are limited. Knowledge-graph retrieval-augmented generation, including K-RagRec, is proposed and studied to address these limitations through knowledge-graph retrieval.

l: lack of up-to-date and domain-specific knowledge, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: is_a significant challenge for LLM-based recommender systems Lack of up-to-date and domain-specific knowledge prevents LLM-based recommender systems from reliably recommending recent films or products and from meeting nuanced recommendation needs. Frequent fine-tuning could address the problem but is computationally expensive and time-consuming.

l: vanilla RAG, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: Vanilla RAG is a RAG method relying on documents and paragraphs; this can add harmful noise and overlook entity relationships, limiting LLM-based recommender reasoning.

l: KG RAG, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: KG RAG retrieves structured knowledge subgraphs to augment an LLM, addressing hallucinations and missing domain knowledge while improving reliability and reasoning in LLM-based recommendations.

l: knowledge vector database, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: knowledge vector database stores indexed knowledge sub-graph representations and retrieves top-K similar sub-graphs using item representations.

l: retrieved knowledge sub-graphs, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: Knowledge sub-graphs are retrieved structures from knowledge graphs that represent an entity and its neighborhood at a specified hop level. They are indexed from item knowledge graphs at coarse and fine granularities and stored in a knowledge vector database. For recommendation, relevant sub-graphs are retrieved, reranked, graph-encoded, and converted or used to augment prompts, prioritizing useful structural information, reducing long context inputs, enhancing recommendations, and helping alleviate hallucinations in language models.

l: GNN Encoder, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: GNN Encoder is a technology in K-RagRec that aggregates neighbor information into hop-level knowledge sub-graph representations, encodes retrieved and re-ranked sub-graphs, and is trained with a second graph neural network. A projector aligns representations with the LLM’s semantic space for knowledge-augmented recommendation.

l: MLP projector, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: MLP projector maps encoded knowledge sub-graph embeddings into the large language model embedding space, aligning semantic spaces through parameters learned during training.

l: structured and faithful knowledge, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: is_retrieved_from knowledge graphs [for enhancing generations] Recent studies focus on retrieving structured and faithful knowledge from graphs to address the limitations of standard RAG. This knowledge is used to enhance generation and has potential for recommendation systems.

l: Retrieve-Rewrite-Answer, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: Retrieve-Rewrite-Answer is an inference-only method proposed by Wu et al. that retrieves knowledge-graph sub-graphs, converts them into text for recommendation, and has limited accuracy and slower reported efficiency than K-RagRec.

l: G-Retriever, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: retrieves sub-graphs [from various types of graphs] G-retriever is a prompt-tuning retrieval baseline. It is competitive with GraphToken w/ RAG but is generally outperformed by K-RagRec and requires 5.86 seconds per inference on MovieLens-1M with LLama-2-7b.

l: recommendations, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: Recommendations use RAG with language models and book or movie knowledge. An under-explored, promising direction is retrieving faithful structured knowledge from knowledge graphs. K-RagRec retrieves knowledge sub-graphs to help select a user’s preferred item from candidates containing one positive and multiple negative samples.

l: methodology, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: describes K-RagRec [in this work] The methodology introduces the notation and concepts used by K-RagRec and describes each component of the framework. It defines the knowledge graph, LLM-based recommendations, indexing, retrieval, re-ranking, recommendation, and optimization procedures.

l: LLM-based recommender systems, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: LLM-based recommender systems model user preferences from historical interactions and item side information, then use a frozen large language model to select preferred items from candidate sets. Their central challenge is intelligent selective retrieval; popularity-based retrieval improves efficiency, while future work targets policies that update as interests change.

l: user, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: A user is represented through a sequence of historical item interactions, such as clicks or purchases. The user’s historical items are included in the recommendation prompt and are used to identify relevant knowledge sub-graphs.

l: item (K-RagRec's item), Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: has side information [such as title and description] An item can have publicly available side information, including a title and description, which is used to model user preferences and form retrieval queries. Items are also evaluated by popularity to determine whether knowledge augmentation is needed.

l: hop-field knowledge sub-graphs, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: Hop-field knowledge sub-graphs support semantic indexing, aggregate multiple-hop neighborhoods into coarse and fine structures, provide node views, and capture effects missed by first-order retrieval.

l: semantic indexing, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: Semantic indexing uses a pre-trained language model and graph neural network to represent knowledge sub-graphs, stores them in a knowledge vector database, and enables coarse and fine-grained retrieval.

l: popularity selective retrieval policy, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: Popularity selective retrieval policy determines whether items in LLM-based recommender systems are augmented with retrieved knowledge, using item popularity. It retrieves items below a predefined popularity threshold, helping cold-start items with limited knowledge while reducing retrieval time. In the main experiments, the threshold is 50%. As the threshold increases, recommendation performance initially improves but later declines, and inference time rises almost linearly. The policy therefore balances retrieval efficiency, knowledge augmentation, and performance; reinforcement learning may later update it dynamically.

l: knowledge sub-graphs retrieval, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: Knowledge sub-graphs retrieval embeds a query item’s text attributes with the indexing language model, retrieves the top-K most similar sub-graphs from a knowledge vector database, and forms retrieved sub-graphs for historical items.

l: knowledge sub-graphs re-ranking, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: Knowledge sub-graphs re-ranking compares a recommendation prompt with retrieved sub-graph representations, selects top-N relevant sub-graphs, and reduces information overload to improve recommendation retrieval quality.

l: knowledge-augmented recommendation, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: uses knowledge sub-graph [as a soft prompt for the large language model] Knowledge-augmented recommendation encodes the re-ranked knowledge sub-graphs with a graph neural network and maps their representations into the large language model’s embedding space. The resulting embedding is appended as a soft prompt before the input token embeddings.

l: pre-trained language model, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: captures semantic information [for nodes] The pre-trained language model captures semantic information from node attributes, relation attributes, item text attributes, and recommendation prompts. The same model is used for indexing, retrieval, and re-ranking so that the representations remain in a consistent embedding space.

l: popularity, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: Popularity is measured by sales volume and page views, and a predefined threshold determines whether items require knowledge graph retrieval.

l: soft prompt tuning, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: Soft prompt tuning trains K-RagRec by using retrieved knowledge sub-graphs as soft graph prompts, updating graph neural networks and MLP projector with cross-entropy loss while freezing large language model.

l: MovieLens-1M, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: is_a movie rating dataset [approximately one million ratings] MovieLens-1M contains approximately one million movie ratings and movie title descriptions. It is used for evaluating recommendation accuracy, recall, ablations, efficiency, and parameter choices for K-RagRec.

l: MovieLens-20M, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: is_a movie rating dataset [over 20 million ratings from more than 138,000 users on 27,000 movies] MovieLens-20M contains more than 20 million ratings from over 138,000 users across 27,000 movies. K-RagRec obtains strong recommendation results on this dataset and uses a four-layer Graph Transformer configuration.

l: Amazon Book, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: is_a book recommendation dataset [more than 10 million user ratings] Amazon Book records more than 10 million book ratings and book titles. K-RagRec is evaluated on it, and removing the GNN Encoder decreases accuracy by 45.9% in the reported ablation study.

l: Freebase, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: Freebase is an external knowledge graph used for recommendation tasks. It supplies filtered triples to reconstruct knowledge graphs for MovieLens-1M, MovieLens-20M, and Amazon Book experiments, and is the study’s only external source before proposed use of YAGO, DBpedia, and Wikipedia.

l: KAPING, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: KAPING is an inference-only method proposed by Baek et al. that retrieves knowledge-graph triples, with limited accuracy and 6.47-second inference.

l: PT w/ KG-Text, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: PT w/ KG-Text is a prompt-tuning approach augmented with KG-Text retrieval. It generally performs below the other retrieval-based prompt-tuning methods and K-RagRec.

l: GraphToken w/ RAG, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: GraphToken w/ RAG is a prompt-tuning retrieval baseline. It improves over PT w/ KG-Text in the reported comparisons but generally remains below K-RagRec.

l: Lora w/ KG-Text, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: is_a LoRA fine-tuning approach [with retrieval] Lora w/ KG-Text applies LoRA fine-tuning with the naive KG-Text retrieval approach. Lora w/ K-RagRec improves over it across the reported datasets, backbones, and metrics.

l: Lora w/ K-RagRec, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: is_a LoRA fine-tuning approach [using K-RagRec] Lora w/ K-RagRec combines LoRA fine-tuning with K-RagRec retrieval. It achieves the best performance in the fine-tuning comparisons across most reported settings.

l: LLama-2-7b, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: is_a backbone LLM LLama-2-7b is one of the backbone language models used in the experiments. With this backbone, K-RagRec shows especially large improvements over the strongest prompt-tuning baselines and is evaluated in the efficiency and ablation studies.

l: LLama-3-8b, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: is_a backbone LLM LLama-3-8b is used as a backbone language model for evaluating the retrieval and fine-tuning methods. K-RagRec improves over the strongest prompt-tuning baselines across the reported datasets and metrics.

l: QWEN2-7b, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: is_a backbone LLM QWEN2-7b is used as a backbone language model in the comparison experiments. K-RagRec improves over the strongest prompt-tuning baselines across the reported datasets, with the largest gains generally appearing in Accuracy and Recall@3.

l: Accuracy, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: is_a evaluation metric Accuracy measures whether the model selects the target item from a pool of 20 candidates containing one target and 19 randomly sampled items. K-RagRec records higher Accuracy than the compared prompt-tuning retrieval baselines in the main experiments.

l: Recall@k, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: is_a evaluation metric [reported for k equal to 3 and 5] Recall@k evaluates whether the target item is ranked within the top k predictions, with k set to 3 and 5. For trained models, it is computed from the probability assigned to each candidate item.

l: knowledge graph retrieval for recommendation, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: Knowledge graph retrieval for recommendation is evaluated through methods that retrieve triples, sub-graphs, or encoded graph information to augment language models. The experiments find that K-RagRec's selective retrieval and graph encoding provide stronger recommendation performance and lower inference cost than the compared approaches.

l: large language model recommendation, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: Large language model recommendation is evaluated using historical user interactions to predict a preferred item from a candidate pool. The study compares inference-only, prompt-tuned, and LoRA-fine-tuned language model recommendation systems.

l: prompt tuning, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: Prompt tuning is evaluated with KG-Text retrieval, GraphToken with RAG, G-retriever, and K-RagRec. K-RagRec generally outperforms the other prompt-tuning retrieval methods in the reported experiments.

l: LoRA fine-tuning, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: LoRA fine-tuning is evaluated with both KG-Text and K-RagRec retrieval. Combining LoRA fine-tuning with K-RagRec produces the strongest results in most reported settings.

l: knowledge-graph RAG, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: is_investigated_for LLM-based recommendations [in this pioneering study] Knowledge-graph RAG is the subject of a pioneering study investigating its use for LLM-based recommendations. The study identifies the need to assess it with larger models and additional knowledge graphs.

l: proposed framework, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: A proposed framework, evaluated only on 7b and 8b models due to GPU constraints, uses Freebase and popularity to select retrieved items.

l: 7b and 8b models, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: The 7b and 8b models were the only model sizes used to evaluate the framework because of GPU resource constraints. Future work plans to extend the method to larger models to assess its effectiveness and scalability.

l: popularity-based retrieval, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation
s: improves retrieval efficiency [by determining which items to retrieve] Popularity-based retrieval is used to determine which items to retrieve and to improve retrieval efficiency. Future work may replace or extend it with more flexible mechanisms that adapt to changes in user interest.

l: MAIN-RAG: Multi-Agent Filtering Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: This is a long paper in the Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, presenting MAIN-RAG, or Multi-Agent Filtering Retrieval-Augmented Generation, by Chia-Yuan Chang, Zhimeng Jiang, Vineeth Rakesh, Menghai Pan, Chin-Chia Michael Yeh, Guanchu Wang, Mingzhi Hu, Zhichao Xu, Yan Zheng, Mahashweta Das, and Na Zou. The paper addresses a central weakness of retrieval-augmented generation: although retrieval can ground Large Language Model responses in external, real-time information, retrieved sets often contain irrelevant or noisy documents that mislead models, lower reliability, and add computation. After motivating this problem and situating it among training-based and training-free RAG methods, the paper formalizes queries, retrieved documents, relevance scores, rankings, adaptive thresholds, and filtered document sets. It then introduces the training-free MAIN-RAG pipeline. Agent-1, the Predictor, produces answers using individual documents. Agent-2, the Judge, evaluates Document-Query-Answer Triplets with Yes/No judgments; relevance is measured by the difference between the log probabilities of “Yes” and “No.” These scores filter and reorder documents. Agent-3, the Final-Predictor, generates the final answer from the retained, ordered evidence. A query-specific adaptive judge bar is based on average document scores and can be adjusted with the candidate set’s standard deviation. Experiments in zero-shot settings compare MAIN-RAG with retrieval and non-retrieval baselines on ARC-Challenge, TriviaQA-unfiltered, PopQA, and ALCE-ASQA. Using three pre-trained LLM agents and a Contriever-MS MARCO retriever, MAIN-RAG generally surpasses the listed training-free and non-retrieval systems; MAIN-RAG-Llama38B has the strongest reported results among listed training-free systems. The reported gains are 2–11% in answer accuracy, alongside fewer irrelevant documents and more consistent responses. Ablations support the default adaptive judge bar and descending document order, though case studies show both successful and unsuccessful filtering. The paper concludes that multi-agent filtering and ranking improve relevant-information recall while limiting noise. It proposes finer-grained thresholds, uses beyond question answering, and human feedback or tuning-based filtering as future work. It also notes environmental risk from LLM inference and retrieved-document workflows, and seeks to reduce repetitive experiments through controlled settings.
